entries.a3be41d81202f174d3dcbfe2b89707db78477bee: <div sID="gen19023" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="32" osisID="Ezek.32" sID="Ezek.32"/> <div eID="gen19023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19024" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19025" type="x-p"/> Still we are upon the destruction of Pharaoh and Egypt, which is wonderfully enlarged upon, and with a great deal of emphasis. When we read so very much of Egypt's ruin, no less than six several prophecies at divers times delivered concerning it, we are ready to think, Surely there is some special reason for it. And, I. Perhaps it may look as far back as the book of Genesis, where we find (<reference osisRef="Ezek.15.14">ch. xv. 14</reference>) that God determined to judge Egypt for oppressing his people; and, though that was in part fulfilled in the plagues of Egypt and the drowning of Pharaoh, yet, in this destruction, here foretold, those old scores were reckoned for, and that was to have its full accomplishment. II. Perhaps it may look as far forward as the book of the Revelation, where we find that the great enemy of the gospel-church, that makes war with the Lamb, is spiritually called Egypt, <reference osisRef="Rev.11.8">Rev. xi. 8</reference>. And, if so, the destruction of Egypt and its Pharaoh was a type of the destruction of that proud enemy; and between this prophecy of the ruin of Egypt and the prophecy of the destruction of the antichristian generation there is some analogy. We have two distinct prophecies in this chapter relating to Egypt, both in the same month, one on the 1st day, the other that day fortnight, probably both on the sabbath day. They are both lamentations, not only to signify how lamentable the fall of Egypt should be, but to intimate how much the prophet himself should lament it, from a generous principle of love to mankind. The destruction of Egypt is here represented under two similitudes:—1. The killing of a lion, or a whale, or some such devouring creature, <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.1-Ezek.32.16">ver. 1-16</reference>. 2. The funeral of a great commander or captain-general, <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.17-Ezek.32.32">ver. 17-32</reference>. The two prophecies of this chapter are much of the same length.
entries.73f17b6047565df6e6964973d599caf93916d818: <div eID="gen19025" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19024" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Fall of Egypt; Lamentation for Pharaoh. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 587.)</title> <div sID="gen19026" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass in the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, in the first <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Son of man, take up a lamentation for Pharaoh king of Egypt, and say unto him, Thou art like a young lion of the nations, and thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> as a whale in the seas: and thou camest forth with thy rivers, and troubledst the waters with thy feet, and fouledst their rivers. <hi type="super">3</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; I will therefore spread out my net over thee with a company of many people; and they shall bring thee up in my net. <hi type="super">4</hi> Then will I leave thee upon the land, I will cast thee forth upon the open field, and will cause all the fowls of the heaven to remain upon thee, and I will fill the beasts of the whole earth with thee. <hi type="super">5</hi> And I will lay thy flesh upon the mountains, and fill the valleys with thy height. <hi type="super">6</hi> I will also water with thy blood the land wherein thou swimmest, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to the mountains; and the rivers shall be full of thee. <hi type="super">7</hi> And when I shall put thee out, I will cover the heaven, and make the stars thereof dark; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give her light. <hi type="super">8</hi> All the bright lights of heaven will I make dark over thee, and set darkness upon thy land, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <hi type="super">9</hi> I will also vex the hearts of many people, when I shall bring thy destruction among the nations, into the countries which thou hast not known. <hi type="super">10</hi> Yea, I will make many people amazed at thee, and their kings shall be horribly afraid for thee, when I shall brandish my sword before them; and they shall tremble at <hi type="italic">every</hi> moment, every man for his own life, in the day of thy fall. <hi type="super">11</hi> For thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; The sword of the king of Babylon shall come upon thee. <hi type="super">12</hi> By the swords of the mighty will I cause thy multitude to fall, the terrible of the nations, all of them: and they shall spoil the pomp of Egypt, and all the multitude thereof shall be destroyed. <hi type="super">13</hi> I will destroy also all the beasts thereof from beside the great waters; neither shall the foot of man trouble them any more, nor the hoofs of beasts trouble them. <hi type="super">14</hi> Then will I make their waters deep, and cause their rivers to run like oil, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <hi type="super">15</hi> When I shall make the land of Egypt desolate, and the country shall be destitute of that whereof it was full, when I shall smite all them that dwell therein, then shall they know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">16</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the lamentation wherewith they shall lament her: the daughters of the nations shall lament her: they shall lament for her, <hi type="italic">even</hi> for Egypt, and for all her multitude, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <div eID="gen19026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19027" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The prophet is ordered to <hi type="italic">take up a lamentation for Pharaoh king of Egypt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.2">v. 2</reference>. It concerns ministers to be much of a serious spirit, and, in order thereunto, to be frequent in taking up lamentations for the fall and ruin of sinners, as those that have not desired, but dreaded, the woeful day. Note, Ministers that would affect others with the things of God must make it appear that they are themselves affected with the miseries which sinners bring upon themselves by their sins. It becomes us to weep and tremble for those that will not weep and tremble for themselves, to try if thereby we may set them a weeping, set them a trembling. <div eID="gen19027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19028" type="x-p"/> II. He is ordered to show cause for that lamentation. <div eID="gen19028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19029" type="x-p"/> 1. Pharaoh has been a troubler of the nations, even of his own nation, which he should have procured the repose of: He is <hi type="italic">like a young lion of the nations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.2">v. 2</reference>), loud and noisy, hectoring and threatening as a lion when he roars. Great potentates, if they by tyrannical and oppressive, are in God's account no better than beasts of prey. He is like <hi type="italic">a whale,</hi> or dragon, like a crocodile (so some) <hi type="italic">in the seas,</hi> very turbulent and vexatious, as the <hi type="italic">leviathan</hi> that <hi type="italic">makes the deep to boil like a pot,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.41.31">Job xli. 31</reference>. When Pharaoh engaged in an unnecessary war with the Cyrenians he <hi type="italic">came forth with his rivers,</hi> with his armies, <hi type="italic">troubled the waters,</hi> disturbed his own kingdom and the neighbouring nations, <hi type="italic">fouled the rivers,</hi> and made them muddy. Note, A great deal of disquiet is often given to the world by the restless ambition and implacable resentments of proud princes. Ahab is he that troubles Israel, and not Elijah. <div eID="gen19029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19030" type="x-p"/> 2. He that has troubled others must expect to be himself troubled; for the Lord is righteous, <reference osisRef="Josh.7.25">Josh. vii. 25</reference>. <div eID="gen19030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19031" type="x-p"/> (1.) This is set forth here by a comparison. Is Pharaoh like a <hi type="italic">great whale,</hi> which, when it comes up the river, gives great disturbance, a leviathan which Job cannot <hi type="italic">draw out with a hook?</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.41.1">Job xli. 1</reference>), yet God has a net for him which is large enough to enclose him and strong enough to secure him (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will spread my net over thee,</hi> even the army of the Chaldeans, a <hi type="italic">company of many people;</hi> they shall force him out of his fastnesses, dislodge him out of his possessions, throw him like a great fish upon dry ground, <hi type="italic">upon the open field</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.4">v. 4</reference>), where being out of his element, he must die of course, and be a prey to the birds and beasts, as was foretold, <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.5">ch. xxix. 5</reference>. What can the strongest fish do to help itself when it is out of the water and lies gasping? <hi type="italic">The flesh</hi> of this great whale shall be <hi type="italic">laid upon the mountains</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.5">v. 5</reference>) and the <hi type="italic">valleys</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">filled with his height.</hi> Such numbers of Pharaoh's soldiers shall be slain that the dead bodies shall be scattered upon the hills and there shall be heaps of them piled up in the valleys. Blood shall be shed in such abundance as to swell the rivers in the valleys. Or, Such shall be the bulk, such the height, of this leviathan, that, when he is laid upon the ground, he shall fill a valley. Such vast quantities of blood shall issue from this <hi type="italic">leviathan</hi> as shall <hi type="italic">water the land of Egypt,</hi> the land wherein <hi type="italic">now he swims,</hi> now he sports himself, <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.6">v. 6</reference>. It shall reach <hi type="italic">to the mountains,</hi> and the waters of Egypt shall again be <hi type="italic">turned into blood</hi> by this means: <hi type="italic">The rivers shall be full of thee.</hi> The judgments executed upon Pharaoh of old are expressed by the <hi type="italic">breaking</hi> of <hi type="italic">the heads of leviathan in the waters,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.74.13-Ps.74.14">Ps. lxxiv. 13, 14</reference>. But now they go further; this old serpent not only has now his head bruised, but is all crushed to pieces. <div eID="gen19031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19032" type="x-p"/> (2.) It is set forth by a prophecy of the deep impression which the destruction of Egypt should make upon the neighbouring nations; it would put them all into a consternation, as the fall of the Assyrian monarchy did, <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.15-Ezek.31.16">ch. xxxi. 15, 16</reference>. When Pharaoh, who had been like a blazing burning torch, is <hi type="italic">put out</hi> and <hi type="italic">extinguished</hi> it shall make all about him look black, <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.7">v. 7</reference>. The heavens shall be hung with black, the <hi type="italic">stars darkened,</hi> the sun eclipsed, and the moon be deprived of her borrowed light. It is from the upper world that this lower receives its light; and therefore (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.8">v. 8</reference>), when the <hi type="italic">bright lights of heaven</hi> are <hi type="italic">made dark</hi> above, darkness by consequence is <hi type="italic">set upon the land,</hi> upon the earth; so it shall be on the land of Egypt. Here the plague of darkness, which was upon Egypt of old for three days, seems to be alluded to, as, before, the turning of the waters into blood. For, when former judgments are forgotten, it is just that they should be repeated. When their privy-counsellors, and statesmen, and those that have the direction of the public affairs, are deprived of wisdom and made fools, and the things that belong to their peace are hidden from their eyes, then their lights are darkened and the land is in a mist. This is foretold, <reference osisRef="Isa.19.13">Isa. xix. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">The princes of Zoan have become fools.</hi> Now upon the spreading of the report of the fall of Egypt, and the bringing of the news to remote countries, <hi type="italic">countries which they had not known</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.9">v. 9</reference>), people shall be much affected, and shall feel themselves sensibly touched by it. [1.] It shall fill them with vexation to see such an ancient, wealthy, potent kingdom thus humbled and brought down, and the pride of worldly glory, which they have such a value for, stained. The <hi type="italic">hearts of many people</hi> will be <hi type="italic">vexed</hi> to see the word of the God of Israel fulfilled in the destruction of Egypt, and that all the <hi type="italic">gods of Egypt</hi> were not able to relieve it. Note, The destruction of some wicked people is a vexation to others. [2.] It shall fill them with admiration (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.10">v. 10</reference>): They shall be <hi type="italic">amazed at thee,</hi> shall wonder to see such <hi type="italic">great riches</hi> and power <hi type="italic">come to nothing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.18.17">Rev. xviii. 17</reference>. Note, Those that admire with complacency the pomp of this world will admire with consternation the ruin of that pomp, which to those that know the vanity of all things here below is no surprise at all. [3.] It shall fill them with fear: even <hi type="italic">their kings</hi> (that think it their prerogative to be secure) shall be <hi type="italic">horribly afraid for thee,</hi> concluding their own house to be in danger when their neighbour's is on fire. <hi type="italic">When I shall brandish my sword before them they shall tremble every man for his own life.</hi> Note, When the sword of God's justice is drawn against some, to cut them off, it is thereby brandished before others, to give them warning. And those that will not be admonished by it, and made to reform, shall yet be frightened by it, and made to tremble. They shall <hi type="italic">tremble at every moment, because of thy fall.</hi> When others are ruined by sin we have reason to quake for fear, as knowing ourselves guilty and obnoxious. <hi type="italic">Who is able to stand before this holy Lord God?</hi> <div eID="gen19032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19033" type="x-p"/> (3.) It is set forth by a plain and express prediction of the desolation itself that should come upon Egypt. [1.] The instruments of the desolation appear here very formidable. It is the <hi type="italic">sword of the king of Babylon,</hi> that warlike, that victorious prince, that shall <hi type="italic">come upon thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.11">v. 11</reference>), the <hi type="italic">swords of the mighty,</hi> even the <hi type="italic">terrible of the nations, all of them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.12">v. 12</reference>), an army that there is no standing before. Note, Those that delight in war, and are upon all occasions entering into contention, may expect, some time or other, to be engaged with those that will prove too hard for them. Pharaoh had been forward to quarrel with his neighbour and to come forth <hi type="italic">with his rivers,</hi> with his armies, <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.2">v. 2</reference>. But God will now give him enough of it. [2.] The instances of the desolation appear here very frightful, much the same with what we had before, <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.10-Ezek.29.12">ch. xxix. 10-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.7">xxx. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The multitude of Egypt shall be destroyed, not decimated, some picked out to be made examples, but all cut off. Note, The numbers of sinners, though they be a multitude, will neither secure them against God's power nor entitle them to his pity. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The pomp of Egypt shall be spoiled, the pomp of their court, what they have been proud of. Note, in renouncing the pomps of this world we did ourselves a great kindness, for they are things that are soon spoiled and that cheat their admirers. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The cattle of Egypt, that used to feed by the rivers, shall be destroyed (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.13">v. 13</reference>), either cut off by the sword or carried off for a prey. Egypt was famous for horses, which would be an acceptable booty to the Chaldeans. The rivers shall be no more frequented as they have been by man and beast, that came thither to drink. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> The <hi type="italic">waters of Egypt,</hi> that used to flow briskly, shall now grow deep, and slow, and heavy, and shall <hi type="italic">run like oil</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.14">v. 14</reference>), a figurative expression signifying that there should be such universal sadness and heaviness upon the whole nation that even the rivers should go softly and silently like mourners, and quite forget their rapid motion. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> The whole country of Egypt shall be stripped of its wealth; it shall be <hi type="italic">destitute of what whereof it was full</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.15">v. 15</reference>), corn, and cattle, and all the pleasant fruits of the earth; when those are <hi type="italic">smitten that dwell therein</hi> the ground is untilled, and that which is gathered becomes an easy prey to the invader. Note, God can soon empty those of this world's goods that have the greatest fulness of those things and are full of them, that enjoy most and have their hearts set upon those enjoyments. The Egyptians were full of their pleasant and plentiful country, and its rich productions. Every one that talked with them might perceive how much it filled them. But God can soon make their <hi type="italic">country destitute of that whereof it is full;</hi> it is therefore our wisdom to be full of treasures in heaven. When the country is made destitute, 1. It shall be an instruction to them: <hi type="italic">Then shall they know that I am the Lord.</hi> A sensible conviction of the vanity of the world, and the fading perishing nature of all things in it, will contribute much to our right knowledge of God as our portion and happiness. 2. It shall be a lamentation to all about them: <hi type="italic">The daughters of the nations shall lament her</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.16">v. 16</reference>), either because, being in alliance with her, they share in her grievances and suffer with her, or, being admirers of her, they at least share in her grief and sympathize with her. They shall lament <hi type="italic">for Egypt and all her multitude;</hi> it shall excite their pity to see so great a devastation made. By enlarging the matters of our joy we increase the occasions of our sorrow.
entries.8373d9fcf37beab9e0058e0459d0ad8fdb9df5ff: <div eID="gen19033" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Fall of Egypt; Egypt's Destruction Completed. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 587.)</title> <div sID="gen19034" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> It came to pass also in the twelfth year, in the fifteenth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">18</hi> Son of man, wail for the multitude of Egypt, and cast them down, <hi type="italic">even</hi> her, and the daughters of the famous nations, unto the nether parts of the earth, with them that go down into the pit. <hi type="super">19</hi> Whom dost thou pass in beauty? go down, and be thou laid with the uncircumcised. <hi type="super">20</hi> They shall fall in the midst of <hi type="italic">them that are</hi> slain by the sword: she is delivered to the sword: draw her and all her multitudes. <hi type="super">21</hi> The strong among the mighty shall speak to him out of the midst of hell with them that help him: they are gone down, they lie uncircumcised, slain by the sword. <hi type="super">22</hi> Asshur <hi type="italic">is</hi> there and all her company: his graves <hi type="italic">are</hi> about him: all of them slain, fallen by the sword: <hi type="super">23</hi> Whose graves are set in the sides of the pit, and her company is round about her grave: all of them slain, fallen by the sword, which caused terror in the land of the living. <hi type="super">24</hi> There <hi type="italic">is</hi> Elam and all her multitude round about her grave, all of them slain, fallen by the sword, which are gone down uncircumcised into the nether parts of the earth, which caused their terror in the land of the living; yet have they borne their shame with them that go down to the pit. <hi type="super">25</hi> They have set her a bed in the midst of the slain with all her multitude: her graves <hi type="italic">are</hi> round about him: all of them uncircumcised, slain by the sword: though their terror was caused in the land of the living, yet have they borne their shame with them that go down to the pit: he is put in the midst of <hi type="italic">them that be</hi> slain. <hi type="super">26</hi> There <hi type="italic">is</hi> Meshech, Tubal, and all her multitude: her graves <hi type="italic">are</hi> round about him: all of them uncircumcised, slain by the sword, though they caused their terror in the land of the living. <hi type="super">27</hi> And they shall not lie with the mighty <hi type="italic">that are</hi> fallen of the uncircumcised, which are gone down to hell with their weapons of war: and they have laid their swords under their heads, but their iniquities shall be upon their bones, though <hi type="italic">they were</hi> the terror of the mighty in the land of the living. <hi type="super">28</hi> Yea, thou shalt be broken in the midst of the uncircumcised, and shalt lie with <hi type="italic">them that are</hi> slain with the sword. <hi type="super">29</hi> There <hi type="italic">is</hi> Edom, her kings, and all her princes, which with their might are laid by <hi type="italic">them that were</hi> slain by the sword: they shall lie with the uncircumcised, and with them that go down to the pit. <hi type="super">30</hi> There <hi type="italic">be</hi> the princes of the north, all of them, and all the Zidonians, which are gone down with the slain; with their terror they are ashamed of their might; and they lie uncircumcised with <hi type="italic">them that be</hi> slain by the sword, and bear their shame with them that go down to the pit. <hi type="super">31</hi> Pharaoh shall see them, and shall be comforted over all his multitude, <hi type="italic">even</hi> Pharaoh and all his army slain by the sword, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <hi type="super">32</hi> For I have caused my terror in the land of the living: and he shall be laid in the midst of the uncircumcised with <hi type="italic">them that are</hi> slain with the sword, <hi type="italic">even</hi> Pharaoh and all his multitude, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <div eID="gen19034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19035" type="x-p"/> This prophecy concludes and completes the burden of Egypt, and leaves it and all its multitude in the pit of destruction. <div eID="gen19035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19036" type="x-p"/> I. We are here invited to attend the funeral of that once flourishing kingdom, to lament its fall, and to take a view of those who attend it to the grave and accompany it in the grave. <div eID="gen19036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19037" type="x-p"/> 1. This dead corpse of a kingdom is here brought to the grave. The prophet is ordered to <hi type="italic">cast them down</hi> to the pit (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.18">v. 18</reference>), to foretel their destruction as one that had authority, as Jeremiah was set over the kingdoms, <reference osisRef="Jer.1.10">Jer. i. 10</reference>. He must speak in God's name, and as from him who will cast them down. Yet he must foretel it as one that had an affectionate concern for them; he must <hi type="italic">wail for the multitude of Egypt,</hi> even when he <hi type="italic">casts them down.</hi> When Egypt is slain, let her have an honourable funeral, befitting her quality; let her be buried <hi type="italic">with the daughters of the famous nations,</hi> in their burying-places and with the same ceremony. It is but a poor allay to the reproach and terror of death to be buried with those that were famous; yet this is all that is allowed to Egypt. Shall Egypt think to exempt herself from the common fate of proud and imperious nations? No; she must take her lot with them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.19">v. 19</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Whom dost thou surpass in beauty?</hi> Art thou so much fairer than any other nation that thou shouldst expect therefore to be excused? No; others as fair as thou have sunk into the pit; <hi type="italic">go down</hi> therefore, and <hi type="italic">be thou laid with the uncircumcised.</hi> Thou art like them and art likely to lie among them. The multitude of Egypt shall all <hi type="italic">fall in the midst of those that are slain with the sword,</hi> now that there is a general slaughter made among the nations." Egypt with the rest must drink of the bloody cup, and therefore she is <hi type="italic">delivered to the sword,</hi> to the sword of war (but, in God's hand, the sword of justice), is delivered to be publicly executed. <hi type="italic">Draw her and all her multitude;</hi> draw them either as the dead bodies of great men are drawn in honour to the grave, in a hearse, or as malefactors are drawn in disgrace to the place of execution, on a sledge; draw them to the pit, and let them be made a spectacle to the world. <div eID="gen19037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19038" type="x-p"/> 2. This corpse of a kingdom is bid welcome to the grave, and Pharaoh is made free of the congregation of the dead, and admitted into their regions, not without some pomp and ceremony. As the surprising fall of the king of Babylon is thus illustrated, <hi type="italic">Hell from beneath is moved for thee to meet thee at thy coming,</hi> and to introduce thee into those mansions of darkness (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.9">Isa. xiv. 9</reference>, &c.), so here (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.21">v. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">They shall speak to him out of the midst of hell,</hi> as it were congratulating his arrival and calling him to join with them in acknowledging that which neither he nor they would be brought to own when they were in their pomp and pride, that it is in vain to think of contesting with God, and none ever hardened their hearts against him and prospered. They shall say to him, and to those that pretended to help him, Where are you now? What have you brought your attempts to at last? Divers nations are here mentioned as gone down to the grave before Egypt that are ready to give her a scornful reception and upbraid her with coming to them at last. These nations here spoken of were probably such as had been of late years ruined and wasted by the king of Babylon, and their princes cut off; let Egypt know that she has <hi type="italic">neighbour's fare.</hi> When she goes to the grave she does but <hi type="italic">migrare ad plures—migrate to the majority;</hi> there are <hi type="italic">innumerable before her.</hi> But it is observable that though Judah and Jerusalem were just about this time, or a little before, utterly ruined and laid waste, yet they are not mentioned here among the nations that welcome Egypt to the pit; for though they suffered the same things that these nations suffered, and by the same hand, yet the kind intentions of their affliction, and its happy issue at last, and the mercy God had yet in reserve for them, altered the property of it; it was not to them a <hi type="italic">going down to the pit,</hi> as it was to the heathen; they were not <hi type="italic">smitten as others were,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">slain according to the slaughter of other nations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.27.7">Isa. xxvii. 7</reference>. But let us see who those are that have <hi type="italic">gone to the grave</hi> before Egypt, that <hi type="italic">lie uncircumcised, slain by the sword,</hi> with whom she must now take up her lodging. (1.) There lie the Assyrian empire, and all the princes and mighty men of that monarchy (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">Asshur is there and all her company,</hi> all the countries that were tributaries to and had dependence upon that crown. That mighty potentate who used to lie in state, with his guards and grandees about him, now lies in obscurity, with his <hi type="italic">graves about him</hi> and his soldiers in them, unable any longer to do him service or honour; they are <hi type="italic">all of them slain, fallen by the sword.</hi> The number of their months was <hi type="italic">cut off in the midst,</hi> and, being <hi type="italic">bloody</hi> and <hi type="italic">deceitful men,</hi> they were not suffered to <hi type="italic">live out half their days.</hi> Their <hi type="italic">braves were set in the sides of the pit,</hi> all in a row, like beds in a common chamber, <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.23">v. 23</reference>. All their company is such as were <hi type="italic">slain, fallen by the sword;</hi> a vast congregation there is of such, who had <hi type="italic">caused terror in the land of the living.</hi> But as the death of those to whom they were a terror put an end to their fears (in the grave <hi type="italic">the prisoners rest together</hi> and <hi type="italic">hear not the voice of the oppressor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.3.18">Job iii. 18</reference>), so the death of these mighty men puts an end to their terrors. Who is afraid of <hi type="italic">a dead lion?</hi> Note, Death will be a king of terrors to those who, instead of making themselves blessings, make themselves terrors, in their generation. (2.) There lies the kingdom of Persia, which perhaps within the memory of man at that time had been wasted and brought down: <hi type="italic">There is Elam and all her multitude,</hi> the king of Elam and his numerous armies, <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.24-Ezek.32.25">v. 24, 25</reference>. They also had <hi type="italic">caused their terror in the land of the living,</hi> had made a fearful noise and bluster among the nations in their day. But Elam has now a grave by herself, and the graves of the common people <hi type="italic">round about her, fallen by the sword;</hi> she has <hi type="italic">her bed in the midst of the slain</hi> that went down <hi type="italic">uncircumcised, unsanctified,</hi> unholy, and not in covenant with God. They have <hi type="italic">borne their shame with those that go down to the pit;</hi> they have fallen under the common disgrace and mortification of mankind, that they die and are buried; nay, they die under particular marks of ignominy, which God and man put upon them. Note, Those who cause their terror shall, sooner or later, bear their <hi type="italic">shame,</hi> and be made a terror to themselves. The king of Elam is <hi type="italic">put in the midst of those that are slain.</hi> All the honour he can now pretend to is to be buried in the chief sepulchre. (3.) There lies the Scythian power, which, about this time, was busy in the world. <hi type="italic">Meshech</hi> and <hi type="italic">Tubal,</hi> those barbarous northern nations, had lately made a descent upon the Medes, and <hi type="italic">caused their terror</hi> among them, lived among them upon free quarter for some years, making every thing their own that they could lay their hands on; but at length Cyaxares, king of the Medes, drew them by a wile into his power, but off abundance of them, and obliged them to quit his country, <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.26">v. 26</reference>. There lie Meshech and Tubal, and all their multitude; there is a burying place for them, with their chief commander in the midst of them, <hi type="italic">all of them uncircumcised, slain by the sword.</hi> These Scythians, dying ingloriously as they lived, are not laid, as the other nations spoken of before, in the bed of honour (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall not lie with the mighty,</hi> shall not be buried in state, as those are, even by consent of the enemy, that are slain in the field of battle, that <hi type="italic">go down to their graves with their weapons of war</hi> carried before the hearse, or trailed after it, that have particularly <hi type="italic">their swords laid under their heads,</hi> as if they could sleep the sweeter in the grave when they laid their heads on such a pillow. These Scythians are not buried with these marks of honour, but <hi type="italic">their iniquities shall be upon their sons;</hi> they shall, for their iniquity, be left unburied, though they were the <hi type="italic">terror</hi> even <hi type="italic">of the mighty in the land of the living.</hi> (4.) There lies the kingdom of Edom, which had flourished long, but about this time, at least before the destruction of Egypt, was made quite desolate, as was foretold, <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.13">ch. xxv. 13</reference>. Among the sepulchres of the nations <hi type="italic">there is Edom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.29">v. 29</reference>. There lie, not dignified with monuments or inscriptions, but mingled with common dust, <hi type="italic">her kings and all her princes,</hi> her wise statesmen (which Edom was famous for), and her brave soldiers. These <hi type="italic">with their might are laid by those that were slain by the sword;</hi> their might could not prevent it, nay, their might helped to procure it, for that both encouraged them to engage in war and incensed their neighbours against them, who thought it necessary to curb their growing greatness. A great deal of pains they took to ruin themselves, as many do, who <hi type="italic">with their might,</hi> with all their might, are <hi type="italic">laid by those that were slain with the sword.</hi> The Edomites retained circumcision, being of the seed of Abraham. But that shall stand them in no stead; they shall <hi type="italic">lie with the uncircumcised.</hi> (5.) There lie the <hi type="italic">princes of the north, and all the Zidonians.</hi> These were as well acquainted with maritime affairs as the Egyptians were, who relied much upon that part of their strength, but they have <hi type="italic">gone down with the slain</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.30">v. 30</reference>), down to the pit. Now they are <hi type="italic">ashamed of their might,</hi> ashamed to think how much they boasted of it and trusted to it; and, as the <hi type="italic">Edomites with their might,</hi> so these <hi type="italic">with their terror,</hi> are laid with those that are <hi type="italic">slain by the sword</hi> and are forced to take their lot with them. They <hi type="italic">bear their shame with those that go down to the pit,</hi> die in as much disgrace as those that are cut off by the hand of public justice. (6.) All this is applied to Pharaoh and the Egyptians, who have no reason to flatter themselves with hopes of tranquillity when they see how the wisest, and wealthiest, and strongest, of their neighbours have been laid waste (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.28">v. 28</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Yea, thou shalt be broken in the midst of the uncircumcised;</hi> when God is pulling down the unhumbled and unreformed nations thou must expect to come down with them." [1.] It will be some extenuation of the miseries of Egypt to observe that it has been the case of so many great and mighty nations before (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">Pharaoh shall see them and be comforted;</hi> it will be some ease to his mind that he is not the first king that has been slain in battle—his not the first army that has been routed, his not the first kingdom that has been made desolate. Mr. Greenhill observes here, "The comfort which wicked ones have after death is poor comfort, not real, but imaginary." They will find little satisfaction in having so many fellow-sufferers; the rich man in hell dreaded it. It is only in point of honour that Pharaoh can <hi type="italic">see and be comforted.</hi> [2.] But nothing will be an exemption from these miseries; for (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.32">v. 32</reference>) <hi type="italic">I have caused my terror in the land of the living.</hi> Great men have caused their terror, have studied how to make every body <hi type="italic">fear them. Oderint dum metuant—Let them hate, so that they do but fear.</hi> But now the great God has <hi type="italic">caused his terror in the land of the living;</hi> and therefore he laughs at theirs, because he sees that <hi type="italic">his day is coming,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.37.13">Ps. xxxvii. 13</reference>. In this day of terror Pharaoh <hi type="italic">and all his multitude</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">laid with those that are slain by the sword.</hi> <div eID="gen19038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19039" type="x-p"/> II. The view which this prophecy gives us of ruined states may show us something, 1. Of this present world, and the empire of death in it. Come, and see the calamitous state of human life; see what a dying world this is. The strong die, the mighty die, Pharaoh and all his multitude. See what a killing world this is. They are all <hi type="italic">slain with the sword.</hi> As if men did not die fast enough of themselves, men are ingenious at finding out ways to destroy one another. It is not only a great pit, but a great cock-pit. 2. Of the other world. Though it is the destruction of nations as such that perhaps is principally intended here, yet here is a plain allusion to the final and everlasting ruin of impenitent sinners, of those that are uncircumcised in heart; they are <hi type="italic">slain by the sword</hi> of divine justice; their <hi type="italic">iniquity is upon them,</hi> and with it they <hi type="italic">bear their shame.</hi> Those, Christ's enemies, that would not have him to reign over them, <hi type="italic">shall be brought forth</hi> and <hi type="italic">slain before him,</hi> though they be as pompous, though they be as numerous, as Pharaoh and <hi type="italic">all his multitude.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ezek.32"/> <div eID="gen19039" type="x-p"/>

entries.81ed23d96096a5d8ce271b190ac79fbf9fc4f066: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11626"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 32</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.32.1-Ezek.32.32">Eze 32:1-32</reference>. Two Elegies over Pharaoh, One Delivered on the First Day (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.1">Eze 32:1</reference>), THE Other on the Fifteenth Day of the Same Month, the Twelfth of the Twelfth Year.</title> <div sID="gen21062" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11626"/>1. The twelfth year from the carrying away of Jehoiachin; Jerusalem was by this time overthrown, and Amasis was beginning his revolt against Pharaoh-hophra. <div eID="gen21062" type="x-p"/>
entries.94c9c982d89fce5d0a01c886fe0694bfd9a188ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11627"/><div sID="gen21063" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11627"/><hi type="bold">2. Pharaoh--</hi>"Phra" in Burmah, signifies the king, high priest, and idol.<div eID="gen21063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21064" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whale--</hi>rather, any monster of the waters; here, the crocodile of the Nile. Pharaoh is as a lion on dry land, a crocodile in the waters; that is, an object of terror everywhere.<div eID="gen21064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21065" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">camest forth with thy rivers--</hi>"breakest forth" [Fairbairn]. The antithesis of "seas" and "rivers" favors Grotius rendering, "Thou camest forth from the sea into the rivers"; that is, from thy own empire into other states. However, English Version is favored by the "thy": thou camest forth with thy rivers (that is, with thy forces) and with thy feet didst fall irrecoverably; so Israel, once desolate, troubles the waters (that is, neighboring states). <div eID="gen21065" type="x-p"/>
entries.779fc829be6c940bfd14e363289e8c9dc6a7cd18: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11628"/><div sID="gen21066" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11628"/><hi type="bold">3. with a company of many people--</hi>namely, the Chaldeans (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.3">Eze 29:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.7.12">Ho 7:12</reference>).<div eID="gen21066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21067" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my net--</hi>for they are My instrument. <div eID="gen21067" type="x-p"/>
entries.7c6f807504ef35ae12d8b9fa614adcd2d09cb558: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11629"/><div sID="gen21068" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11629"/><hi type="bold">4. leave thee upon the land--</hi>as a fish drawn out of the water loses all its strength, so Pharaoh (in <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.3">Eze 32:3</reference>, compared to a water monster) shall be (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.5">Eze 29:5</reference>). <div eID="gen21068" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb6c75b1a946316dd54bdebfdba3d80ac762aac5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11630"/><div sID="gen21069" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11630"/><hi type="bold">5. thy height--</hi>thy hugeness [Fairbairn]. The great heap of corpses of thy forces, on which thou pridest thyself. "Height" may refer to mental elevation, as well as bodily [Vatablus]. <div eID="gen21069" type="x-p"/>
entries.8338630765acd7d2edd6fdc3d5db7b370e84b971: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11631"/><div sID="gen21070" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11631"/><hi type="bold">6. land wherein thou swimmest--</hi>Egypt: the land watered by the Nile, the the source of its fertility, wherein thou swimmest (carrying on the image of the crocodile, that is, wherein thou dost exercise thy wanton power at will). Irony. The land shall still afford seas to swim in, but they shall be seas of blood. Alluding to the plague (<reference osisRef="Exod.7.19">Ex 7:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.8.8">Re 8:8</reference>). Havernick translates, "I will water the land with what flows from thee, even thy blood, reaching to the mountains": "with thy blood overflowing even to the mountains." Perhaps this is better. <div eID="gen21070" type="x-p"/>
entries.28266efdbd95220500aed00119e226e1e40523c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11632"/><div sID="gen21071" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11632"/><hi type="bold">7. put thee out--</hi>extinguish thy light (<reference osisRef="Job.18.5">Job 18:5</reference>). Pharaoh is represented as a bright star, at the extinguishing of whose light in the political sky the whole heavenly host is shrouded in sympathetic darkness. Here, too, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.6">Eze 32:6</reference>, there is an allusion to the supernatural darkness sent formerly (<reference osisRef="Exod.10.21-Exod.10.23">Ex 10:21-23</reference>). The heavenly bodies are often made images of earthly dynasties (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.10">Is 13:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.29">Mt 24:29</reference>). <div eID="gen21071" type="x-p"/>
entries.be09cb175c22c98bc7b6e874d044b628d52f4d09: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11633"/><div sID="gen21072" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11633"/><hi type="bold">9. thy destruction--</hi>that is, tidings of thy destruction (literally, "thy breakage") carried by captive and dispersed Egyptians "among the nations" [Grotius]; or, thy broken people, resembling one great fracture, the ruins of what they had been [Fairbairn]. <div eID="gen21072" type="x-p"/>
entries.a2d42eae71d7b926ebc753942f5fd9165b935a86: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11634"/><div sID="gen21073" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11634"/><hi type="bold">10. brandish my sword before them--</hi>literally, "in their faces," or sight. <div eID="gen21073" type="x-p"/>
entries.bd8fd951f6178db28f26717a6dd51fbc7dd95149: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11635"/><div sID="gen21074" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11635"/>13. (See on <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.11">Eze 29:11</reference>). The picture is ideally true, not to be interpreted by the letter. The political ascendency of Egypt was to cease with the Chaldean conquest [Fairbairn]. Henceforth Pharaoh must figuratively no longer trouble the waters by man or beast, that is, no longer was he to flood other peoples with his overwhelming forces. <div eID="gen21074" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc0d889aa9ebc45a5a00194c26ef999b555c3af6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11636"/><div sID="gen21075" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11636"/><hi type="bold">14. make their waters deep--</hi>rather, "make ... to subside"; literally, "sink" [Fairbairn].<div eID="gen21075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21076" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">like oil--</hi>emblem of quietness. No longer shall they descend violently on other countries as the overflowing Nile, but shall be still and sluggish in political action. <div eID="gen21076" type="x-p"/>
entries.7b899d96970a1d38b484ad62513075be133378ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11637"/><div sID="gen21077" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11637"/>16. As in <reference osisRef="Ezek.19.14">Eze 19:14</reference>. This is a prophetical lamentation; yet so it shall come to pass [Grotius]. <div eID="gen21077" type="x-p"/>
entries.6d5bb25f24baa5675895c0373aaeb8c47ba44c99: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11638"/><div sID="gen21078" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11638"/>17. The second lamentation for Pharaoh. This funeral dirge in imagination accompanies him to the unseen world. Egypt personified in its political head is ideally represented as undergoing the change by death to which man is liable. Expressing that Egypt's supremacy is no more, a thing of the past, never to be again.<div eID="gen21078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21079" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the month--</hi>the twelfth month (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.1">Eze 32:1</reference>); fourteen days after the former vision. <div eID="gen21079" type="x-p"/>
entries.e09d82cf0ada71b78d05df5b83ddf09117311074: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11639"/><div sID="gen21080" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11639"/><hi type="bold">18. cast them down--</hi>that is, predict that they shall be cast down (so <reference osisRef="Jer.1.10">Jr 1:10</reference>). The prophet's word was God's, and carried with it its own fulfilment.<div eID="gen21080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21081" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">daughters of ... nations--</hi>that is, the nations with their peoples. Egypt is to share the fate of other ancient nations once famous, now consigned to oblivion: Elam (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.24">Eze 32:24</reference>), Meshech, &c. (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.26">Eze 32:26</reference>), Edom (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.29">Eze 32:29</reference>), Zidon (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.30">Eze 32:30</reference>). <div eID="gen21081" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ca5ab59869a598ecf48309dd350e42ce5ef8436: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11640"/><div sID="gen21082" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11640"/><hi type="bold">19. Whom dost thou pass in beauty?--</hi>Beautiful as thou art, thou art not more so than other nations, which nevertheless have perished.<div eID="gen21082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21083" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">go down, &c.--</hi>to the nether world, where all "beauty" is speedily marred. <div eID="gen21083" type="x-p"/>
entries.f9e3dcd039981628989d2fda1b32c1ded634051d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11641"/><div sID="gen21084" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11641"/><hi type="bold">20. she is delivered to the sword--</hi>namely, by God.<div eID="gen21084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21085" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">draw her--</hi>as if addressing her executioners: drag her forth to death. <div eID="gen21085" type="x-p"/>
entries.64b8053b1bcec2681a445a70f4e0b8c2a65bd7f7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11642"/><div sID="gen21086" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11642"/>21. (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.16">Eze 31:16</reference>). Ezekiel has before his eyes <reference osisRef="Isa.14.9">Is 14:9</reference>, &c.<div eID="gen21086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21087" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall speak to him--</hi>with "him" join "with them that help him"; shall speak to him and his helpers with a taunting welcome, as now one of themselves. <div eID="gen21087" type="x-p"/>
entries.327d9209f7925f6d200348df30f8b287c45c5975: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11643"/><div sID="gen21088" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11643"/><hi type="bold">22. her ... his--</hi>The abrupt change of gender is, because Ezekiel has in view at one time the kingdom (feminine), at another the monarch. "Asshur," or Assyria, is placed first in punishment, as being first in guilt. <div eID="gen21088" type="x-p"/>
entries.0a3b95edc00e99f0871810c76fda4e869cd851a4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11644"/><div sID="gen21089" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11644"/><hi type="bold">23. in the sides of the pit--</hi>Sepulchres in the East were caves hollowed out of the rock, and the bodies were laid in niches formed at the sides. Maurer needlessly departs from the ordinary meaning, and translates, "extremities" (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.14.13">Is 14:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.15">15</reference>).<div eID="gen21089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21090" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which caused terror--</hi>They, who alive were a terror to others, are now, in the nether world, themselves a terrible object to behold. <div eID="gen21090" type="x-p"/>
entries.26137d4fedfa1e4ee7bfefed2ce07737f907c292: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11645"/><div sID="gen21091" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11645"/><hi type="bold">24. Elam--</hi>placed next, as having been an auxiliary to Assyria. Its territory lay in Persia. In Abraham's time an independent kingdom (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.1">Ge 14:1</reference>). Famous for its bowmen (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.6">Is 22:6</reference>).<div eID="gen21091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21092" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">borne their shame--</hi>the just retribution of their lawless pride. Destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.34-Jer.49.38">Jr 49:34-38</reference>). <div eID="gen21092" type="x-p"/>
entries.bca295ef87ab745aa1d13dc45a22628521547f47: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11646"/><div sID="gen21093" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11646"/><hi type="bold">25. a bed--</hi>a sepulchral niche.<div eID="gen21093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21094" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all ... slain by ... sword, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.21">Eze 32:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.24">23, 24</reference>). The very monotony of the phraseology gives to the dirge an awe-inspiring effect. <div eID="gen21094" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c55c5e2f6a8410a73abf91bdd072370f25b7237: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11647"/><div sID="gen21095" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11647"/><hi type="bold">26. Meshech, Tubal--</hi>northern nations: the Moschi and Tibareni, between the Black and Caspian Seas. Herodotus [3.94], mentions them as a subjugated people, tributaries to Darius Hystaspes (see <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.13">Eze 27:13</reference>). <div eID="gen21095" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb7a4f052b0aead770081696e1a7c41acf46aa9f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11648"/><div sID="gen21096" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11648"/><hi type="bold">27. they shall not lie with the mighty--</hi>that is, they shall not have separate tombs such as mighty conquerors have: but shall all be heaped together in one pit, as is the case with the vanquished [Grotius]. Havernick reads it interrogatively, "Shall they not lie with the mighty that are fallen?" But English Version is supported by the parallel (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.18">Is 14:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.19">19</reference>), to which Ezekiel refers, and which represents them as not lying as mighty kings lie in a grave, but cast out of one, as a carcass trodden under foot.<div eID="gen21096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21097" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with ... weapons of war--</hi>alluding to the custom of burying warriors with their arms (1 Maccabees 13:29). Though honored by the laying of "their swords under their heads," yet the punishment of "their iniquities shall be upon their bones." Their swords shall thus attest their shame, not their glory (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.52">Mt 26:52</reference>), being the instruments of their violence, the penalty of which they are paying. <div eID="gen21097" type="x-p"/>
entries.e6e6175d0523f484c7164e5fa2c350691eab2be2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11649"/><div sID="gen21098" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11649"/><hi type="bold">28. Yea, thou--</hi>Thou, too, Egypt, like them, shalt lie as one vanquished. <div eID="gen21098" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ca6cb71581732af11488d6b5629e210f7abfdf9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11650"/><div sID="gen21099" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11650"/><hi type="bold">29. princes--</hi>Edom was not only governed by kings, but by subordinate "princes" or "dukes" (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.40">Ge 36:40</reference>).<div eID="gen21099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21100" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with their might--</hi>notwithstanding their might, they shall be brought down (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.5">Is 34:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.34.10-Isa.34.17">10-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.7">Jr 49:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.13-Jer.49.18">13-18</reference>).<div eID="gen21100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21101" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lie with the uncircumcised--</hi>Though Edom was circumcised, being descended from Isaac, he shall lie with the uncircumcised; much more shall Egypt, who had no hereditary right to circumcision. <div eID="gen21101" type="x-p"/>
entries.6675d96866948d1f5350856b36ed6c551ba3ee6f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11651"/><div sID="gen21102" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11651"/><hi type="bold">30. princes of the north--</hi>Syria, which is still called by the Arabs the north; or the Tyrians, north of Palestine, conquered by Nebuchadnezzar (Eze 26:1-28:26), [Grotius].<div eID="gen21102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21103" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zidonians--</hi>who shared the fate of Tyre (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.21">Eze 28:21</reference>).<div eID="gen21103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21104" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with their terror they are ashamed of their might--</hi>that is, notwithstanding the terror which they inspired in their contemporaries. "Might" is connected by Maurer thus, "Notwithstanding the terror which resulted from their might." <div eID="gen21104" type="x-p"/>
entries.9ac5c7a79405305ef370579a0cb72de44ccd2285: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11652"/><div sID="gen21105" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11652"/><hi type="bold">31. comforted--</hi>with the melancholy satisfaction of not being alone, but of having other kingdoms companions in his downfall. This shall be his only comfort--a very poor one! <div eID="gen21105" type="x-p"/>
entries.73372e815e4458fdbfe1f42079b61a8749c834c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11653"/><div sID="gen21106" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11653"/><hi type="bold">32. my terror--</hi>the Margin or Keri. The Hebrew text or Chetib is "his terror," which gives good sense (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.25">Eze 32:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.30">30</reference>). "My terror" implies that God puts His terror on Pharaoh's multitude, as they put "their terror" on others, for example, under Pharaoh-necho on Judea. As "the land of the living" was the scene of "their terror," so it shall be God's; especially in Judea, He will display His glory to the terror of Israel's foes (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.20">Eze 26:20</reference>). In Israel's case the judgment is temporary, ending in their future restoration under Messiah. In the case of the world kingdoms which flourished for a time, they fall to rise no more. <chapter eID="Ezek.32"/>

entries.9413f476feeef5986c7cfc0fd2d9889f0da60214: <div eID="gen32196" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen32197" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32198" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32198" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32197" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32199" type="x-p"/> The prophet goes on to predict the fall of the king of Egypt, under the figure of an animal of prey, such as a lion or crocodile, caught, slain, and his carcass left a prey to the fowls and wild beasts, <reference osisRef="Eze.32.1-Eze.32.6">Eze 32:1-6</reference>. The figure is then changed; and the greatness of his fall (described by the darkening of the sun, moon, and stars) strikes terror into all the surrounding nations, <reference osisRef="Eze.32.7-Eze.32.10">Eze 32:7-10</reference>. The prophet adds, that the overthrow of the then reigning Egyptian dynasty was to be effected by the instrumentality of the king of Babylon, who should leave Egypt so desolate, that its waters, (alluding to the metaphor used in the second verse), should run as pure and smooth as oil, without the foot of man or the hoof of a beast to disturb them, <reference osisRef="Eze.32.11-Eze.32.16">Eze 32:11-16</reference>. A beautiful, nervous, and concise description of a land ruined and left utterly desolate. In the remaining part of the chapter the same event is pourtrayed by one of the boldest figures ever attempted in any composition, and which at the. same time is executed with astonishing perspicuity and force. God is introduced ordering a place in the lower regions for the king of Egypt and his host, <reference osisRef="Eze.32.17">Eze 32:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.32.18">Eze 32:18</reference>. The prophet delivers his message, pronounces their fate, and commands those who buried the slain to drag him and his multitudes to the subterraneous mansions, <reference osisRef="Eze.32.19">Eze 32:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.32.20">Eze 32:20</reference>. At the tumult and commotion which this mighty work occasions, the infernal shades are represented as roused from their couches to learn the cause. They see and congratulate the king of Egypt, on his arrival among them, <reference osisRef="Eze.32.21">Eze 32:21</reference>. Pharaoh being now introduced into this immense subterraneous cavern, (see the fourteenth chapter of Isaiah, where a similar imagery is employed), the prophet leads him all around the sides of the pit; shows him the gloomy mansions of former tyrants, tells their names as he goes along; beautifully contrasts their former pomp and destructive ambition, when they were a terror to the surrounding states, with their present most abject and helpless condition; declares that all these oppressors of mankind have not only been cut off out of the land of the living, but have gone down into the grave uncircumcised, that is, they have died in their sins, and therefore shall have no resurrection to eternal life; and concludes with showing Pharaoh the place destined for him in the midst of the uncircumcised, and of them that have been slain by the sword, <reference osisRef="Eze.32.22-Eze.32.32">Eze 32:22-32</reference>. This prophetic ode may be considered as a finished model in that species of writing which is appropriated to the exciting of terror. The imagery throughout is sublime and terrible; and no reader of sensibility and taste can accompany the prophet in this funeral procession, and visit the mansions of Hades, without being impressed with a degree of awe nearly approaching to horror. <div eID="gen32199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32200" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen32200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32201" type="x-p"/> In the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, in the first day of the month - On Wednesday, March 22, the twelfth year of the captivity of Jeconiah, A.M. 3417. <div eID="gen32201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32202" type="x-p"/> Instead of the twelfth year, five of Kennicott's MSS., and eight of De Rossi's, read בעשתי עשרה in the eleventh year. This reading is supported by the Syriac; and is confirmed by an excellent MS. of my own, about four hundred years old.
entries.40c290b8f7d79b70c9569fd6642018d68f437c27: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen32202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32203" type="x-p"/> Thou art like a young lion - and thou art as a whale in the seas - Thou mayest be likened to two of the fiercest animals in the creation; to a lion, the fiercest on the land; to a crocodile, תנים tannim, (see <reference osisRef="Eze.29.3">Eze 29:3</reference>), the fiercest in the waters. It may, however, point out the hippopotamus, as there seems to be a reference to his mode of feeding. He walks deliberately into the water over head, and pursues his way in the same manner; still keeping on his feet, and feeding on the plants, etc., that grow at the bottom. Thus he fouls the water with his feet.
entries.de3716fe11032dbd964e3aacd1539584cf5f80cd: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen32203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32204" type="x-p"/> And fill the valleys with thy height - Some translate, with the worms, which should proceed from the putrefaction of his flesh.
entries.a70b252aa59dc35c36bb3461b2ad29e7511c6642: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen32204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32205" type="x-p"/> The land wherein thou swimmest - Egypt; so called, because intersected with canals, and overflowed annually by the Nile.
entries.f76ba15107af7a784f5c63a7abe604b27f4a52fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen32205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32206" type="x-p"/> I will cover the heaven - Destroy the empire. <div eID="gen32206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32207" type="x-p"/> Make the stars thereof dark - Overwhelm all the dependent states. <div eID="gen32207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32208" type="x-p"/> I will cover the sun - The king himself. <div eID="gen32208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32209" type="x-p"/> And the moon shall not give her light - The queen may be meant, or some state less than the kingdom.
entries.f3d9460f271650e5d2c076832c5e249978a27ad6: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen32209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32210" type="x-p"/> And set darkness upon thy land - As I did when a former king refused to let my people go to the wilderness to worship me. I will involve thee, and thy house, and thy people, and the whole land, in desolation and wo.
entries.75bc02084b202a6d21ed7890dbb4166512ae69e4: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen32210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32211" type="x-p"/> I will also vex the hearts - Even the remote nations, who had no connection with thee, shall be amazed at the judgments which have fallen upon thee.
entries.da83d4ada1d9e9ac004280e5224cffd7a37f485f: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen32211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32212" type="x-p"/> Cause their rivers to run like oil - Bring the whole state into quietness, there being no longer a political hippopotamus to foul the waters - to disturb the peace of the country.
entries.1ae5938b3b95d3be6e89207948eca21f52ae4827: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen32212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32213" type="x-p"/> Shall be destitute of that whereof it was full - Of corn, and all other necessaries of life.
entries.e74e85730e6fa8786f33caed43d66f0e3d0fe3c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen32213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32214" type="x-p"/> In the twelfth year - Two of Kennicott's MSS., one of De Rossi's, and one of my own, (that mentioned <reference osisRef="Eze.32.1">Eze 32:1</reference>), have, in the Eleventh year; and so has the Syriac, as before. This prophecy concerns the people of Egypt.
entries.c1a8711483d4395340a254129813b1384764b5cd: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen32214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32215" type="x-p"/> Cast them down - Show them that they shall be cast down. Proclaim to them a casting down prophecy.
entries.a132fc97d15727dbc8c2338d1934ef6fd0dc62ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen32215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32216" type="x-p"/> Whom dost thou pass in beauty? - How little does it signify, whether a mummy be well embalmed, wrapped round with rich stuff, and beautifully painted on the outside, or not. Go down into the tombs, examine the niches, and see whether one dead carcass be preferable to another.
entries.c73bfb1a80f276bf726f0fb2aace62f2a72a7c02: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen32216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32217" type="x-p"/> Out of the midst of hell - שאול sheol, the catacombs, the place of burial. There is something here similar to <reference osisRef="Isa.14.9">Isa 14:9</reference>, where the descent of the king of Babylon to the state of the dead is described.
entries.6c308c5ad463cf97ac9376c1e973fbbfebf05d1b: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen32217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32218" type="x-p"/> Asshur is there - The mightiest conquerors of the earth have gone down to the grave before thee; there they and their soldiers lie together, all slain by the sword.
entries.f3b6aa35dad998aaff31a90b7c92071589231523: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen32218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32219" type="x-p"/> Whose graves are set in the sides of the pit - Alluding to the niches in the sides of the subterranean caves or burying-places, where the bodies are laid. These are numerous in Egypt.
entries.88fa83174e8e5d0da28ceca30577ec78db498961: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen32219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32220" type="x-p"/> There is Elam - The Elamites, not far from the Assyrians; others think that Persia is meant. It was invaded by the joint forces of Cyaxares and Nebuchadnezzar.
entries.a91dca7456910fbc1f7b984041977cd1ca8f7c92: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen32220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32221" type="x-p"/> There is Meshech, Tubal - See on <reference osisRef="Eze.27.13">Eze 27:13</reference> (note).
entries.83902602ffa34096357a7b4613f08c2b7748b573: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen32221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32222" type="x-p"/> Gone down to hell with their weapons of war - Are buried in their armor and with their weapons lying by their sides. It was a very ancient practice, in different nations, to bury a warrior's weapons in the same grave with himself.
entries.eea45b8024e3ceb6937baaac674bfb4ce4951d64: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen32222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32223" type="x-p"/> There is Edom - All the glory and pomp of the Idumean kings, who also helped to oppress the Israelites, are gone down into the grave. Their kings, princes, and all their mighty men lie mingled with the uncircumcised, not distinguished from the common dead: "Where they an equal honor share, <div eID="gen32223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32224" type="x-p"/> Who buried or unburied are. <div eID="gen32224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32225" type="x-p"/> Where Agamemnon knows no more <div eID="gen32225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32226" type="x-p"/> Than Irus, he condemned before. <div eID="gen32226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32227" type="x-p"/> Where fair Achilles and Thersites lie, <div eID="gen32227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32228" type="x-p"/> Equally naked, poor, and dry."
entries.0731915f6c01214295bc4ebe0531f82e95b8ba98: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen32228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32229" type="x-p"/> There be the princes of the north - The kings of Media and Assyria, and all the Zidonians - the kings of Tyre, Sodom, and Damascus. See Calmet.
entries.94f711ce7e9e01065c6d92fac2e16521192c45ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen32229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32230" type="x-p"/> Pharaoh shall see them - Pharaoh also, who said he was a god, shall be found among the vulgar dead. <div eID="gen32230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32231" type="x-p"/> And shalt be comforted - Shall console himself, on finding that all other proud boasters are in the same circumstances with himself. Here is a reference to a consciousness after death.
entries.9386db470db9e9f0ebb9216bb978bdff7e9f981b: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen32231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32232" type="x-p"/> I have caused my terror in the land of the living - I have spread dismay through Judea, the land of the living God, where the living oracles were delivered, and where the upright live by faith. When Pharaoh-necho came against Josiah, defeated, and slew him at Megiddo, fear and terror were spread through all the land of Judea; and the allusion here is probably to that circumstance. But even he is now laid with the uncircumcised, and is no more to be distinguished from the common dead. <div eID="gen32232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32233" type="x-p"/> Much of the phraseology of this chapter may be illustrated by comparing it with Isaiah 14 (note), where see the notes, which the intelligent reader will do well to consult.  <chapter eID="Ezek.32"/> <div eID="gen32233" type="x-p"/>

entries.fec175c9e652c4e211cd83c8672a7094b7eb2132: <div eID="gen15106" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Lamentations over the Ruin of Pharaoh and His People</title> <div sID="gen15107" type="x-p"/> The chapter contains two lamentations composed at different times: the first, in vv. 1-16, relating to the fall of Pharaoh, which rests upon the prophecy contained in Ezekiel 29:1-16 and <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.20-Ezek.30.26">Eze 30:20-26</reference>; the second, in vv. 17-32, in which the prophecy concerning the casting down of this imperial power into hell (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.14-Ezek.31.17">Eze 31:14-17</reference>) is worked out in elegiac form. <div eID="gen15107" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Lamentation over the King of Egypt</title> <div sID="gen15108" type="x-p"/> Pharaoh, a sea-monster, is drawn by the nations out of his waters with the net of God, and cast out upon the earth. His flesh is given to the birds and beasts of prey to devour, and the earth is saturated with his blood (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.2-Ezek.32.6">Eze 32:2-6</reference>). At his destruction the lights of heaven lose their brightness, and all the nations will be amazed thereat (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.7-Ezek.32.10">Eze 32:7-10</reference>). The king of Babel will come upon Egypt, will destroy both man and beast, and will make the land a desert (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.11-Ezek.32.16">Eze 32:11-16</reference>). - The date given in <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.1">Eze 32:1</reference> - <hi type="italic">”In the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, on the first of the month, the word of Jehovah came to me, saying”</hi> - agrees entirely with the relation in which the substance of the ode itself stands to the prophecies belonging to the tenth and eleventh years in Ezekiel 29:1-16 and <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.20-Ezek.30.26">Eze 30:20-26</reference>; whereas the different date found in the Septuagint cannot come into consideration for a moment.
entries.ab386e4167888121bbd3cc4ad1c559f2b4ef81da: <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.2-Ezek.32.6">Eze 32:2-6</reference> <div eID="gen15108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15109" type="x-p"/> The destruction of Pharoah. - Eze 32:2. <hi type="italic">Son of man, raise a lamentation over Pharaoh the king of Egypt, and say to him, Thou wast compared to a young lion among the nations, and yet wast like a dragon in the sea; thou didst break forth in thy streams, and didst trouble the waters with thy feet, and didst tread their streams.</hi> Eze 32:3. <hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Therefore will I spread out my net over thee in the midst of many nations, that they may draw thee up in my yarn;</hi> Eze 32:4. <hi type="italic">And will cast thee upon the land, hurl thee upon the surface of the field, and will cause all the birds of the heaven to settle upon thee, and the beasts of the whole earth to satisfy themselves with thee.</hi> Eze 32:5. <hi type="italic">Thy flesh will I put upon the mountains, and fill the valleys with thy funeral heap.</hi> Eze 32:6. <hi type="italic">I will saturate the earth with thine outflow of thy blood even to the mountains, and the low places shall become full of thee.</hi> - This lamentation begins, like others, with a picture of the glory of the fallen king. Hitzig objects to the ordinary explanation of the words כּפיר גּוים  נדמיתה, λέοντι ἐθνῶν ὡμοιώθης (lxx), <hi type="italic">leoni gentium assimilatus es</hi> (Vulg.), on the ground that the frequently recurring נדמה would only have this meaning in the present passage, and that נמשׁל, which would then be synonymous, is construed in three other ways, but not with the nominative. For these reasons he adopts the rendering, “lion of the nations, thou belongest to death.” But it would be contrary to the analogy of all the קינות to commence the lamentation with such a threat; and Hitzig’s objections to the ordinary rendering of the words will not bear examination. The circumstance that the <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi> נדמה is only met with here in the sense of ὁμοιοῦσθαι, proves nothing; for דּמה has this meaning in the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>, <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Hithpael</hi>, and the construction of the <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi> with the accusative (not nominative, as Hitzig says) may be derived without difficulty from the construction of the synonymous נמשׁל with כ. But what is decisive in favour of this rendering is the fact that the following clause is connected by means of the adversative ואתּה (but thou), which shows that the comparison of Pharaoh to a תּנּים forms an antithesis to the clause in which he is compared to a young lion. If נדמית 'כּפיר ג contained a declaration of destruction, not only would this antithesis be lost, but the words addressed to it as a lion of the nations would float in the air and be used without any intelligible meaning. The lion is a figurative representation of a powerful and victorious ruler; and כּפיר גּוים is really equivalent to אל גּוים in Eze 31:11. <div eID="gen15109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15110" type="x-p"/> Pharaoh was regarded as a mighty conqueror of the nations, “though he was rather to be compared to the crocodile, which stirs up the streams, the fresh waters, and life-giving springs of the nations most perniciously with mouth and feet, and renders turbid all that is pure” (Ewald). תּנּים, as in Eze 29:3. Ewald and Hitzig have taken offence at the words תּגח בּנהרתיך, “thou didst break forth in thy streams,” and alter בּנהרתיך retla d into בּנחרתיך, with thy nostrils (<reference osisRef="Job.41.12">Job 41:12</reference>); but they have not considered that תּגח would be quite out of place with such an alteration, as גּיח in both the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> and <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> (Jdg 20:33) has only the intransitive meaning to break out. The thought is simply this: the crocodile lies in the sea, then breaks occasionally forth in its streams, and makes the waters and their streams turbid with its feet. Therefore shall Pharaoh also end like such a monster (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.3-Ezek.32.6">Eze 32:3-6</reference>). The guilt of Pharaoh did not consist in the fact that he had assumed the position of a ruler among the nations (Kliefoth); but in his polluting the water-streams, stirring up and disturbing the life-giving streams of the nations. God will take him in His net by a gathering of nations, and cause him to be drawn out of his element upon the dry land, where he shall become food to the birds and beasts of prey (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.4-Ezek.29.5">Eze 29:4-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.12-Ezek.31.13">Eze 31:12-13</reference>). The words 'בּקהל עמּים ר are not to be understood as referring to the nations, as spectators of the event (Hävernick); but ב denotes the instrument, or medium employed, here the persons by whom God causes the net to be thrown, as is evident from the והעלוּך which follows. According to the <hi type="italic">parallelismus</hi> <hi type="italic">membrorum</hi>, the ἁπ. λεγ. רמוּת can only refer to the carcase of the beast, although the source from which this meaning of the word is derived has not yet been traced. There is no worth to be attached to the reading rimowt in some of the codices, as רמּה does not yield a suitable meaning either in the sense of reptile, or in that of putrefaction or decomposed bodies, which has been attributed to it from the Arabic. Under these circumstances we adhere to the derivation from רוּם, to be high, according to which רמוּת may signify a height or a heap, which the context defines as a funeral-pile. צפה, strictly speaking, a participle from צוּף, to flow, that which flows out, the outflow (Hitzig), is not to be taken in connection with ארץ, but is a second object to השׁקיתי; and the appended word מדּמך indicates the source whence the flowing takes place, and of what the outflow consists. אל ההרים, to the mountains, i.e., up to the top of the mountains. The thought in these verses is probably simply this, that the fall of Pharaoh would bring destruction upon the whole of the land of Egypt, and that many nations would derive advantage from his fall.
